summary: Specifies the Unified Memory Space Protocol, an experimental protocol meant to give immediate access to the memory of remote nodes. It is an experiment and not a standard.

eli5.summary: Imagine being able to reach into a friend's pocket from far away as if it were your own. This experiment tried to let a computer look at another computer's memory like that.

questions: what is unified memory space protocol
access remote memory over a network
how does umsp provide transparent memory access
when would you use umsp for distributed systems
subtitle: A network protocol that presents distributed memory as a single 128-bit address space, letting programs access remote memory directly.

tldr.problem: Building distributed systems that share computation and memory across many machines is complex because programs must learn about network topology, convert addresses, and manage communication primitives instead of just reading and writing memory.
tldr.mechanism: UMSP defines a 128-bit unified address space that spans multiple nodes. Programs issue instructions with these 128-bit addresses; the protocol translates them to network operations, manages sessions between nodes, and handles data transfer, memory allocation, and control transfers as if all memory were local.
tldr.outcome: A distributed job can treat memory across all nodes as a single address space and control threads on remote nodes by jumping to remote addresses. It simplifies distributed system development but adds complexity to the virtual machine layer.

facts.label: Session connections
facts.value: One per job per node pair

today: RFC 3018 is an experimental protocol that has not been adopted. The vision of transparent distributed memory access across heterogeneous systems proved impractical because coordinating memory access, consistency, and failure modes across the network requires higher-level abstractions than simple reads and writes. Virtual machine-based distributed computing eventually used different approaches such as message passing or object distribution frameworks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Unified Memory Space Protocol (UMSP) is a network protocol that creates a distributed memory environment. It allows application programs running on different nodes to interact through immediate reading and writing of memory at 128-bit addresses, rather than by exchanging network messages and primitives.

UMSP is designed for systems based on virtual machines (VMs) that execute pseudo-code. Each node runs one or more VMs, and a job (user application) can be distributed across multiple nodes. A single VM can execute multiple tasks, each containing threads of control. The protocol gives each job its own isolated 128-bit address space, segmented so that each node owns a segment.

Unlike traditional network protocols, user code need not be aware of the network or the physical location of memory. It simply executes instructions using 128-bit addresses. The virtual machine translates these into UMSP protocol operations. UMSP uses TCP for reliable delivery and can use UDP for data that does not require acknowledgement.
sections.eli5: UMSP lets a program running on one computer read and write memory on another computer as if it were local memory, using the same simple memory read and write instructions. The protocol handles the network details automatically.

sections.title: System Architecture and Address Model
sections.content:
UMSP is built around a 128-bit distributed address space. Each 128-bit address contains four parts. The first octet is a header field that specifies the address format (the lengths of the node address and memory address within). The next 0 to 12 octets are a free field for local memory control information. Then comes the node address (1 to 13 octets), which identifies which node the memory belongs to. Finally, the memory address (16 to 64 bits depending on the address format) identifies the location within that node's memory.

The address header has fields that specify the address length, the network type (IPv4, IPv6, etc.), and the local memory address size. Three IPv4 address formats are defined: format 4 uses 4-octet node addresses with 16-bit, 24-bit, or 32-bit local addresses. A 128-bit address must identify the given node unambiguously from all other nodes in the system.

UMSP defines a three-layer computing model. A job is a user application distributed across one or more nodes. A task is the job's instantiation on a single node. A thread is a control thread executing within a task. One central Job Control Point (JCP) controls each job and coordinates all tasks. The job has an isolated 128-bit address space; all threads in the job can read and write anywhere in this space.
sections.eli5: The address format packs a destination node and a local memory location into 128 bits. The system separates jobs like different programs, and each job can have pieces running on multiple computers that all share one address space.

sections.title: Instructions and Protocols
sections.content:
UMSP instructions follow a header-extension-operands format. The header is at least 2 octets and at most 16 octets, containing an opcode, flags for compression and chains, and optional request IDs. Extension headers provide additional information such as message data, alignment requirements, or lifetime limits. Operands contain the instruction data.

Operation codes fall into ranges: 1-112 are management instructions, 113-127 are reserved, and 128-223 are instructions for exchange between virtual machines. A compression scheme reduces header overhead when instructions belong to the same session or chain.

The protocol defines instructions for reading and writing data across the 128-bit address space, comparison operations, control transfers (jump and call to remote addresses), memory allocation and deallocation, and working with objects (named associative memory). Instructions can be grouped into sequences, transactions, and fragmented instructions.

Sessions establish TCP connections between nodes for a particular job. A job may have multiple simultaneous session connections to different nodes. The protocol can also work in connectionless mode for certain operations. All instructions travel over TCP or UDP with a SESSION_ID and optional CHAIN_NUMBER to organize them.
sections.eli5: Each instruction has a header with an operation code, optional request IDs to track responses, and data. The protocol supports memory read/write, calling functions on remote machines, managing memory remotely, and even executing transactions across the network.

sections.title: Job Management and Data Exchange
sections.content:
UMSP defines a lifecycle for jobs. A job initiates with a CONTROL_REQ request that the JCP confirms or rejects. Each task registers with a TASK_REG message. Session connections open with SESSION_OPEN and SESSION_ACCEPT exchanges. When work is complete, tasks terminate with TASK_TERMINATE, and the job completes with JOB_COMPLETED.

Data exchange between virtual machines uses a set of instructions: REQ_DATA to request data from a remote address, DATA to return it, and WRITE or WRITE_EXT to store data remotely. Comparison instructions (CMP, CMP_EXT) let a remote machine compare values and report the result. Control transfer instructions (JUMP, CALL, RETURN) let a thread jump to or call code on a remote node, creating a new thread there if needed.

The protocol supports working with objects: named data structures on remote nodes. Instructions like OBJ_REQ_DATA, OBJ_WRITE, and CALL_BNUM read/write object data or execute named procedures within objects. The protocol can also manage memory (MEM_ALLOC, FREE) and move code between nodes (MVCODE, MVRUN).
sections.eli5: A job starts when the JCP accepts it. Each piece running on a node registers as a task. Then the job can read, write, and run code on any node in its address space. Transactions ensure that groups of operations complete together or not at all.

sections.title: Implementation Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
The protocol is designed to work across a wide range of systems: from simple devices with dedicated processors to universal computers and clusters. A minimal profile for simple devices without an operating system is possible. The protocol does not define memory control; that is the responsibility of each node's virtual machine.

Multiple virtual machines on a node may share a common memory space or be completely isolated. The protocol requires reliable delivery from the transport layer and uses TCP by default, but allows other protocols (including connectionless-mode) as long as they meet reliability and ordering requirements. The protocol does not mandate support for multiple threads on a node.

UMSP is connection-oriented at the transport layer. One TCP connection (or multiple with multiplexing) is used between each pair of nodes for a given job. The protocol does not define the transport layer connection control; that is handled externally. The minimal segment size for operation is 6 octets; 54 octets suffices for all functions.
sections.eli5: The protocol is flexible: it can run on big computers or tiny devices. It does not control local memory; the virtual machine does. Different VMs can share memory or be isolated. The protocol relies on TCP to handle the network details.
